1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
4	For quality estimation, all signals achieve positive $\rho$ across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL).
5	Rankings hold across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}); at the capability boundary (WNUT-17), all signals collapse.
6	For selection, LP is the only signal achieving significant gains, and only when both conditions are met: $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD (13.8\% degeneracy, within-instance $\rho{\approx}0.5$, $p{<}0.001$), $+0.42$~pp on SciERC (17.8\%, $\rho{\approx}0.24$, $p{=}0.091$), failure on CoNLL (47.4\%).
7	Structural signals uniformly degrade selection regardless of dataset.
8	RE signal rankings are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
9	
10	\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
11	We identify two mechanisms: \textit{instance degeneracy} (affecting consensus-proximity selection) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (affecting per-sample selection).
12	
13	Within-instance analysis (restricted to non-degenerate instances where F1 varies across samples) reveals that MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} does correlate positively with F1 (SJ median within-instance $\rho{=}0.524$ on SciERC, $0.994$ on CoNLL), and on these instances consensus-proximity selection closes 23\% (SciERC) to 41\% (CoNLL) of the oracle gap.
14	However, approximately 29\% of non-degenerate SciERC instances exhibit \textit{negative} within-instance SJ--F1 correlation, for a substantial minority, higher structural consistency is actively associated with lower quality. This heterogeneity further explains why pooled positive correlation does not translate to reliable MBR selection.
15	Beyond this, fine-tuned models exhibit pervasive \textit{instance degeneracy}: 17.8\% of SciERC instances (47.4\% on CoNLL) produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples, offering zero selection headroom; an additional 13\% (49\% on CoNLL) yield constant utility scores, preventing MBR ranking entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
16	Instance degeneracy is not an artifact of our setup but a consequence of model capability: the better the model, the less room for selection to add value.
17	CoNLL (91\% single-sample F1) exhibits 47.4\% degeneracy; Few-NERD (75\%) shows 13.8\%; SciERC (66\%) shows 17.8\%; WNUT-17 (${\approx}$42\%, macro) shows near-zero.
18	Degeneracy is determined by the interplay of task structure, model architecture, and training convergence. Better models on easier tasks tend toward higher rates (CoNLL 47.4\% vs.\ SciERC 17.8\%), but dataset-specific factors (number of entity types, semantic overlap) and training budget also modulate the outcome (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
19	Scale ablation confirms this tension: Qwen3-8B shows 17.8\% instance degeneracy on SciERC vs.\ 10.4\% for the weaker Qwen3-4B, despite comparable within-instance utility correlation ($\rho{=}0.52$ vs.\ $0.55$; Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
20	Cross-model evidence reinforces the pattern: LLaMA-3.1-8B on CoNLL exhibits 89.2\% degeneracy (vs.\ Qwen3-8B's 47.4\%), consistent with its higher single-sample F1 (0.924 vs.\ 0.908); structural signals retain diagnostic value ($\rho{\approx}0.43$; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}) despite selection being entirely ineffective at this degeneracy level (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
21	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high}, all consensus-proximity variants consistently fail because degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
22	On SciERC, LP selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$; $\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}); on Few-NERD, where degeneracy drops to 13.8\% and LP-quality alignment is strong ($\rho{\approx}0.5$), LP achieves significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}). Both low degeneracy and adequate alignment are required.
23	
24	\begin{table}[t]
25	\centering
26	\small
27	\caption{Instance degeneracy statistics ($T{=}1.0$). ``Constant F1'': all $N$ samples receive identical instance-level F1. ``Constant utility'': MBR (SJ) utility identical across candidates. 4B data confirms degeneracy scales with model capability.}
28	\label{tab:degeneracy}
29	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
30	\toprule
31	& \shortstack{SciERC 8B\\($N{=}8$)} & \shortstack{SciERC 4B\\($N{=}8$)} & \shortstack{CoNLL 8B\\($N{=}16$)} \\
32	\midrule
33	Constant F1 & 17.8\% & 10.4\% & 47.4\% \\
34	Constant utility & 13\% & 7.0\% & 49\% \\
35	Oracle gap closed (non-deg.) & 23\% & 25.2\% & 41\% \\
36	Within-inst.\ SJ $\rho$ (median) & 0.524 & 0.550 & 0.994 \\
37	\bottomrule
38	\end{tabular}
39	\end{table}
40	
41	Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, is severely compressed: median LP range is 0.041 nats (IQR [0.024, 0.073]; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with pooled within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.248$ confirming weak but positive signal.
42	
43	\paragraph{Non-tied subset analysis.}
44	Where compression is mitigated, LP selection works.
45	Restricting to instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied), and LP selection outperforms greedy by $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$).
46	The effect grows monotonically with $\varepsilon$ (full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}), and the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ result survives Bonferroni correction over 5 comparisons.
47	This demonstrates that LP \textit{does} carry per-sample discriminative information; compression, not signal absence, is the bottleneck.
48	However, the effect size is sensitive to subset definition, and the non-tied subset constitutes only 40\% of instances, limiting practical impact.
49	
50	\begin{table}[t]
51	\centering
52	\small
53	\caption{Non-tied subset analysis (SciERC, Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Instances split at LP range $\varepsilon{=}0.05$. Within-instance $\rho$ and selection gain both concentrate in the non-tied subset. Full $\varepsilon$ sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}.}
54	\label{tab:nontied_main}
55	\begin{tabular}{lccc}
56	\toprule
57	Subset & $n$ & $\rho$(LP,F1) & LP $\Delta$ vs.\ greedy \\
58	\midrule
59	Tied (range ${<}0.05$) & 319 & 0.08 & ${\approx}0$ \\
60	Non-tied (range ${\geq}0.05$) & 210 & 0.39 & $+$2.9~pp ($p{=}0.004$) \\
61	\midrule
62	All instances & 529 & 0.248 & $+$0.2~pp ($p{=}0.29$) \\
63	\bottomrule
64	\end{tabular}
65	\end{table}
66	Stratifying by voting confidence reveals a complementary pattern: high-consistency instances (Q4) have collapsed headroom (4.78~pp), leaving nothing to select, while low-consistency instances retain headroom but unreliable LP rankings (Appendix~\ref{app:vc_quartile}).
67	
68	\paragraph{$N$-scaling and temperature.}
69	LP selection improves with $N$, reaching $+0.52$~pp at $N{=}16$ on Few-NERD (paired $p{=}0.003$; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
70	On SciERC, even at $N{=}32$ the best signal captures less than 5\% of available headroom (Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection}).
71	Oracle headroom increases with temperature ($+7.8$~pp at $T{=}0.5$ to $+13.3$~pp at $T{=}1.0$; Table~\ref{tab:t_ablation}), but selection gains remain negligible; the bottleneck lies at the within-instance ranking mechanism.
72	A verbalized confidence baseline confirms that score compression is not LP-specific: the model's self-rated confidence clusters at 8\textendash 9/10 (CoNLL mean 9.24, std 1.32), with the same top-biased pattern regardless of output format (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}; \citealp{bhattacharyya2026beyond}).
73	The free-form RE ablation ($+2.35$~pp, $p{=}0.025$; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}) indicates format constraints contribute to compression in other task types, though NER's own free-form ablation (std ratio 0.97) isolates this as not the primary cause for NER.
74	LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to improve over greedy (best: $+0.2$~pp, $p{>}0.3$); an oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp. Per-sample signal exists, but current signals cannot extract it.
75	Full $N$-scaling, temperature, verbalized confidence, and signal combination analyses are in Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, and~\ref{app:vc_quartile}.
76	
77	\paragraph{Hypotheses for LP compression.}
78	We identify four (non-mutually-exclusive) mechanisms, though we do not isolate their individual contributions.
79	Two are \textit{constraint-imposed}: (b) schema-dominated tokens, where constrained decoding enforces structural tokens that carry no extraction information yet dominate the sequence; and (c) vocabulary restriction, where constrained decoding shrinks the effective vocabulary, concentrating probability mass.
80	Two are \textit{model-learned}: (a) token-level averaging, where mean log-probability over long sequences smooths token-level variance; and (d) format-token dilution, where fine-tuned models assign extremely high LP to schema tokens, diluting the signal from entity-name tokens (free-form parse rates of 99.95\% confirm format tokens dominate).
81	The constraint-imposed mechanisms (b)\textendash (c) predict that free-form decoding should reduce compression; our NER ablation finds negligible change (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), the model-learned mechanisms (a) and (d) are likely the primary drivers for NER.
82	
83	\paragraph{Ablation: free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
84	Removing grammar constraints (SciERC NER, Qwen3-8B, 4 seeds) yields nearly identical LP distributions (std ratio 0.97) and negligible selection changes (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), ruling out constrained decoding as the cause of NER compression.
85	Removing format constraints restores LP selection for RE: bootstrap mean $+2.35$~pp (95\% CI [$+0.24$, $+4.50$], $p{=}0.025$, $n{=}397$), though driven by magnitude asymmetry rather than instance-level win rate (sign test: 45W/45L/307T; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
86	LP selection failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), consistent with a systematic rather than stochastic failure mode.
87	VC tends to select the most typical rather than the best output, consistent with MBR's known mode-seeking bias \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}.
88	All consensus-proximity strategies fail because instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
89	
90	\paragraph{Ablation: entity-token LP.}
91	We directly test hypothesis (d) by isolating entity-mention tokens from the log-probability computation.
92	On SciERC, entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher within-instance variance than full-sequence LP; format tokens do compress the signal.
93	However, entity-token LP selection performs strictly \textit{worse} than full-sequence LP on both datasets ($-2.0$~pp on SciERC, $-3.3$~pp on CoNLL).
94	Entity tokens are either too sparse (5.3\% of sequence tokens on SciERC) for stable estimation, or nearly saturated (79.4\% of instances tied on CoNLL), consistent with CoNLL's limited entity vocabulary (4 types, high-frequency names) that fine-tuning drives to near-deterministic prediction.
95	This rules out format-token dilution as the primary cause and points to an intrinsic pattern: fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities to entity-name tokens themselves, leaving minimal discriminative signal regardless of aggregation scope.
96	Even disaggregating to entity-token logprobs fails to break compression: on CoNLL, 79.4\% of sample pairs share identical entity-token LP. Compression operates at the representation level rather than being diluted by non-entity tokens.
97	
98	\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
99	The correlation-selection gap for structural signals is persistent across all four datasets, but LP selection is degeneracy-gated.
100	At the \textit{low-resource boundary} (WNUT-17, macro F1${\approx}$42\%), QE signals themselves become unreliable: full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}), so selection is moot.
101	At the \textit{ceiling boundary} (CoNLL, F1${\approx}$91\textendash 92\%, degeneracy 47\textendash 89\% across models), selection shows only a marginal structural exception: VC achieves $+0.28$~pp ($p{<}0.03$) at $N{=}16$, capturing ${\sim}$10\% of the 2.5~pp oracle headroom (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}); LP fails entirely.
102	In the \textit{moderate regime}, two conditions jointly determine LP effectiveness: at 17.8\% degeneracy with weak alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.24$; SciERC), LP gains are positive but sub-significant ($+0.42$~pp, $p{=}0.091$); at 13.8\% degeneracy with strong alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$; Few-NERD), LP achieves highly significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}).
103	The cross-dataset gradient (47\% $\to$ fail, 18\% $\to$ weak, 14\% $\to$ strong; $n{=}3$ datasets) is consistent with low degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment being jointly necessary; entity-type-level evidence provides stronger statistical grounding (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
104	When candidates differ sufficiently in quality, LP's per-sample signal can exploit the headroom.
105	The pattern persists at finer granularity: per-entity-type analysis on Few-NERD shows 7/8 types with positive LP gains, the sole exception being the highest-degeneracy type (Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
106	Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy because they rank candidates by typicality, not quality.
107	Whether these patterns persist on larger models (70B+) remains open.
108	Two independent manipulations confirm that alignment is largely determined by task structure rather than generation diversity: reducing LoRA rank from 32 to 8 yields degeneracy of 7.2\% with $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.24$ (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), while increasing temperature to $T{=}1.2$ yields degeneracy of 12.5\% with $\rho{=}0.225$ (Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}).
109	Both approach Few-NERD's degeneracy level (13.8\%) without approaching its alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$). The two necessary conditions vary independently, and degeneracy reduction alone cannot unlock LP selection on datasets with weak alignment.
110	
111	\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
112	The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.
113	Even supervised combination of all five signals (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) fails to close the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}); the information bottleneck is in the signal space accessible to unsupervised aggregation (our five hand-crafted features); whether richer per-token representations (e.g., hidden-state probes) can close the gap is an open question.
114	Effective selection thus requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}, not confidence signal aggregation; $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
115	Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).
116	
117	\paragraph{Practical guidelines for practitioners.}
118	Based on our empirical findings, we suggest a diagnostic workflow for deploying multi-sample selection on new datasets or models.
119	The first step is to estimate dataset-level instance degeneracy on a small labeled subset, using the constant-F1 (gold-filtered) criterion (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}): generate $N$ samples per instance and compute the fraction where all samples receive identical F1.
120	This diagnostic requires only one generation pass and no additional model calls.
121

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{Implications for practitioners.}
For quality estimation, all signals achieve positive $\rho$ across non-collapsed datasets (LP $\rho{=}0.42$ on Few-NERD, VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on SciERC, EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL).
Rankings hold across model families and a 4B ablation (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}); at the capability boundary (WNUT-17), all signals collapse.
For selection, LP is the only signal achieving significant gains, and only when both conditions are met: $+1.36$~pp on Few-NERD (13.8\% degeneracy, within-instance $\rho{\approx}0.5$, $p{<}0.001$), $+0.42$~pp on SciERC (17.8\%, $\rho{\approx}0.24$, $p{=}0.091$), failure on CoNLL (47.4\%).
Structural signals uniformly degrade selection regardless of dataset.
RE signal rankings are reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.

\paragraph{Why the gap exists.}
We identify two mechanisms: \textit{instance degeneracy} (affecting consensus-proximity selection) and \textit{weak LP-quality alignment} (affecting per-sample selection).

Within-instance analysis (restricted to non-degenerate instances where F1 varies across samples) reveals that MBR utility \cite{eikema2022sampling} does correlate positively with F1 (SJ median within-instance $\rho{=}0.524$ on SciERC, $0.994$ on CoNLL), and on these instances consensus-proximity selection closes 23\% (SciERC) to 41\% (CoNLL) of the oracle gap.
However, approximately 29\% of non-degenerate SciERC instances exhibit \textit{negative} within-instance SJ--F1 correlation, for a substantial minority, higher structural consistency is actively associated with lower quality. This heterogeneity further explains why pooled positive correlation does not translate to reliable MBR selection.
Beyond this, fine-tuned models exhibit pervasive \textit{instance degeneracy}: 17.8\% of SciERC instances (47.4\% on CoNLL) produce identical F1 across all $N$ samples, offering zero selection headroom; an additional 13\% (49\% on CoNLL) yield constant utility scores, preventing MBR ranking entirely (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
Instance degeneracy is not an artifact of our setup but a consequence of model capability: the better the model, the less room for selection to add value.
CoNLL (91\% single-sample F1) exhibits 47.4\% degeneracy; Few-NERD (75\%) shows 13.8\%; SciERC (66\%) shows 17.8\%; WNUT-17 (${\approx}$42\%, macro) shows near-zero.
Degeneracy is determined by the interplay of task structure, model architecture, and training convergence. Better models on easier tasks tend toward higher rates (CoNLL 47.4\% vs.\ SciERC 17.8\%), but dataset-specific factors (number of entity types, semantic overlap) and training budget also modulate the outcome (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
Scale ablation confirms this tension: Qwen3-8B shows 17.8\% instance degeneracy on SciERC vs.\ 10.4\% for the weaker Qwen3-4B, despite comparable within-instance utility correlation ($\rho{=}0.52$ vs.\ $0.55$; Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
Cross-model evidence reinforces the pattern: LLaMA-3.1-8B on CoNLL exhibits 89.2\% degeneracy (vs.\ Qwen3-8B's 47.4\%), consistent with its higher single-sample F1 (0.924 vs.\ 0.908); structural signals retain diagnostic value ($\rho{\approx}0.43$; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}) despite selection being entirely ineffective at this degeneracy level (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high}, all consensus-proximity variants consistently fail because degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).
On SciERC, LP selection approximately matches greedy decoding ($T{=}0$; $\Delta{=}{+}0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}); on Few-NERD, where degeneracy drops to 13.8\% and LP-quality alignment is strong ($\rho{\approx}0.5$), LP achieves significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}). Both low degeneracy and adequate alignment are required.

Log-probability, the only per-sample signal, is severely compressed: median LP range is 0.041 nats (IQR [0.024, 0.073]; Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}), with pooled within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.248$ confirming weak but positive signal.

\paragraph{Non-tied subset analysis.}
Where compression is mitigated, LP selection works.
Restricting to instances with LP range ${\geq}0.05$ ($n{=}210$, 40\% of total; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}), within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ rises from 0.08 (tied subset) to 0.39 (non-tied), and LP selection outperforms greedy by $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$).
The effect grows monotonically with $\varepsilon$ (full sweep in Appendix~\ref{app:logprob_ties}), and the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ result survives Bonferroni correction over 5 comparisons.
This demonstrates that LP \textit{does} carry per-sample discriminative information; compression, not signal absence, is the bottleneck.
However, the effect size is sensitive to subset definition, and the non-tied subset constitutes only 40\% of instances, limiting practical impact.

Stratifying by voting confidence reveals a complementary pattern: high-consistency instances (Q4) have collapsed headroom (4.78~pp), leaving nothing to select, while low-consistency instances retain headroom but unreliable LP rankings (Appendix~\ref{app:vc_quartile}).

\paragraph{$N$-scaling and temperature.}
LP selection improves with $N$, reaching $+0.52$~pp at $N{=}16$ on Few-NERD (paired $p{=}0.003$; \S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
On SciERC, even at $N{=}32$ the best signal captures less than 5\% of available headroom (Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection}).
Oracle headroom increases with temperature ($+7.8$~pp at $T{=}0.5$ to $+13.3$~pp at $T{=}1.0$; Table~\ref{tab:t_ablation}), but selection gains remain negligible; the bottleneck lies at the within-instance ranking mechanism.
A verbalized confidence baseline confirms that score compression is not LP-specific: the model's self-rated confidence clusters at 8\textendash 9/10 (CoNLL mean 9.24, std 1.32), with the same top-biased pattern regardless of output format (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}; \citealp{bhattacharyya2026beyond}).
The free-form RE ablation ($+2.35$~pp, $p{=}0.025$; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}) indicates format constraints contribute to compression in other task types, though NER's own free-form ablation (std ratio 0.97) isolates this as not the primary cause for NER.
LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to improve over greedy (best: $+0.2$~pp, $p{>}0.3$); an oracle tiebreaker within VC-equivalent groups recovers $+7.9$~pp. Per-sample signal exists, but current signals cannot extract it.
Full $N$-scaling, temperature, verbalized confidence, and signal combination analyses are in Appendices~\ref{app:n_scaling}, \ref{app:verbalized_confidence}, and~\ref{app:vc_quartile}.

\paragraph{Hypotheses for LP compression.}
We identify four (non-mutually-exclusive) mechanisms, though we do not isolate their individual contributions.
Two are \textit{constraint-imposed}: (b) schema-dominated tokens, where constrained decoding enforces structural tokens that carry no extraction information yet dominate the sequence; and (c) vocabulary restriction, where constrained decoding shrinks the effective vocabulary, concentrating probability mass.
Two are \textit{model-learned}: (a) token-level averaging, where mean log-probability over long sequences smooths token-level variance; and (d) format-token dilution, where fine-tuned models assign extremely high LP to schema tokens, diluting the signal from entity-name tokens (free-form parse rates of 99.95\% confirm format tokens dominate).
The constraint-imposed mechanisms (b)\textendash (c) predict that free-form decoding should reduce compression; our NER ablation finds negligible change (std ratio 0.97; Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), the model-learned mechanisms (a) and (d) are likely the primary drivers for NER.

\paragraph{Ablation: free-form decoding.}\label{sec:ablation}
Removing grammar constraints (SciERC NER, Qwen3-8B, 4 seeds) yields nearly identical LP distributions (std ratio 0.97) and negligible selection changes (Appendix~\ref{app:freeform_ablation}), ruling out constrained decoding as the cause of NER compression.
Removing format constraints restores LP selection for RE: bootstrap mean $+2.35$~pp (95\% CI [$+0.24$, $+4.50$], $p{=}0.025$, $n{=}397$), though driven by magnitude asymmetry rather than instance-level win rate (sign test: 45W/45L/307T; Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}).
LP selection failures show cross-seed stability (Jaccard${=}0.42$; Appendix~\ref{app:lp_failure_stability}), consistent with a systematic rather than stochastic failure mode.
VC tends to select the most typical rather than the best output, consistent with MBR's known mode-seeking bias \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}.
All consensus-proximity strategies fail because instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom that positive within-instance correlation would otherwise exploit (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}; Appendix~\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).

\paragraph{Ablation: entity-token LP.}
We directly test hypothesis (d) by isolating entity-mention tokens from the log-probability computation.
On SciERC, entity-token LP exhibits $4{\times}$ higher within-instance variance than full-sequence LP; format tokens do compress the signal.
However, entity-token LP selection performs strictly \textit{worse} than full-sequence LP on both datasets ($-2.0$~pp on SciERC, $-3.3$~pp on CoNLL).
Entity tokens are either too sparse (5.3\% of sequence tokens on SciERC) for stable estimation, or nearly saturated (79.4\% of instances tied on CoNLL), consistent with CoNLL's limited entity vocabulary (4 types, high-frequency names) that fine-tuning drives to near-deterministic prediction.
This rules out format-token dilution as the primary cause and points to an intrinsic pattern: fine-tuned models assign near-deterministic probabilities to entity-name tokens themselves, leaving minimal discriminative signal regardless of aggregation scope.
Even disaggregating to entity-token logprobs fails to break compression: on CoNLL, 79.4\% of sample pairs share identical entity-token LP. Compression operates at the representation level rather than being diluted by non-entity tokens.

\paragraph{Regime boundaries.}
The correlation-selection gap for structural signals is persistent across all four datasets, but LP selection is degeneracy-gated.
At the \textit{low-resource boundary} (WNUT-17, macro F1${\approx}$42\%), QE signals themselves become unreliable: full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary (VC conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}), so selection is moot.
At the \textit{ceiling boundary} (CoNLL, F1${\approx}$91\textendash 92\%, degeneracy 47\textendash 89\% across models), selection shows only a marginal structural exception: VC achieves $+0.28$~pp ($p{<}0.03$) at $N{=}16$, capturing ${\sim}$10\% of the 2.5~pp oracle headroom (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}); LP fails entirely.
In the \textit{moderate regime}, two conditions jointly determine LP effectiveness: at 17.8\% degeneracy with weak alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.24$; SciERC), LP gains are positive but sub-significant ($+0.42$~pp, $p{=}0.091$); at 13.8\% degeneracy with strong alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$; Few-NERD), LP achieves highly significant gains ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}).
The cross-dataset gradient (47\% $\to$ fail, 18\% $\to$ weak, 14\% $\to$ strong; $n{=}3$ datasets) is consistent with low degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment being jointly necessary; entity-type-level evidence provides stronger statistical grounding (Spearman $\rho{=}{-}0.881$, $p{=}0.004$, $n{=}8$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
When candidates differ sufficiently in quality, LP's per-sample signal can exploit the headroom.
The pattern persists at finer granularity: per-entity-type analysis on Few-NERD shows 7/8 types with positive LP gains, the sole exception being the highest-degeneracy type (Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy because they rank candidates by typicality, not quality.
Whether these patterns persist on larger models (70B+) remains open.
Two independent manipulations confirm that alignment is largely determined by task structure rather than generation diversity: reducing LoRA rank from 32 to 8 yields degeneracy of 7.2\% with $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){=}0.24$ (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}), while increasing temperature to $T{=}1.2$ yields degeneracy of 12.5\% with $\rho{=}0.225$ (Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}).
Both approach Few-NERD's degeneracy level (13.8\%) without approaching its alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$). The two necessary conditions vary independently, and degeneracy reduction alone cannot unlock LP selection on datasets with weak alignment.

\paragraph{Methodological implications.}
The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal.
Even supervised combination of all five signals (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) fails to close the oracle gap (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}); the information bottleneck is in the signal space accessible to unsupervised aggregation (our five hand-crafted features); whether richer per-token representations (e.g., hidden-state probes) can close the gap is an open question.
Effective selection thus requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}, not confidence signal aggregation; $N{=}8$ captures most quality estimation benefit (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
Structural signals are robust to domain shift when the training schema subsumes the target (Appendix~\ref{app:ood}).

\paragraph{Practical guidelines for practitioners.}
Based on our empirical findings, we suggest a diagnostic workflow for deploying multi-sample selection on new datasets or models.
The first step is to estimate dataset-level instance degeneracy on a small labeled subset, using the constant-F1 (gold-filtered) criterion (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}): generate $N$ samples per instance and compute the fraction where all samples receive identical F1.
This diagnostic requires only one generation pass and no additional model calls.

In the high-degeneracy regime (${>}$30\%, exemplified by CoNLL at 47.4\%), LP selection offers no benefit over greedy decoding (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}), and we recommend greedy as the default.
Structural signals nevertheless retain diagnostic value in this regime: SJ and VC achieve $\rho{=}0.43$--$0.47$ on CoNLL (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}), sufficient to flag low-quality extractions for human review.
In the low-degeneracy regime (${<}$15\%, exemplified by Few-NERD at 13.8\%), LP selection is effective when LP-quality alignment is adequate ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$): Few-NERD yields $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$; Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}), and gains scale with $N$ ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, $p{=}0.003$).
The intermediate regime (15--30\%, exemplified by SciERC at 17.8\%) requires further assessment of within-instance LP-quality alignment.
On SciERC, where this alignment is weak ($\rho{\approx}0.24$), LP selection yields only $+0.42$~pp ($p{=}0.091$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}), a gain that does not justify the $N{\times}$ compute cost.

Temperature provides a controllable lever for the first condition: on SciERC, degeneracy falls monotonically from 40.3\% at $T{=}0.5$ to 12.5\% at $T{=}1.2$ (Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}).
However, temperature cannot address the second condition: within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ remains at 0.225 even at $T{=}1.2$, far below Few-NERD's ${\sim}$0.5.
LP-quality alignment appears to be largely determined by task structure (entity vocabulary size, semantic overlap) rather than generation diversity, and remains relatively stable across training configurations (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
Training convergence offers a second lever: on Few-NERD, extending training from 3 to 5 epochs raises degeneracy from 11\% to 31\% while halving LP selection gains ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound}).
Alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (median within-instance $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with degeneracy being the primary bottleneck while alignment acts as a secondary gate.
This is single-dataset evidence; whether the pattern generalizes to other benchmarks requires further investigation.
Practitioners who observe low degeneracy but weak LP alignment should therefore prefer greedy decoding and invest the compute budget in quality estimation for selective prediction instead; for quality estimation alone ($\rho$ up to 0.45), $N{=}8$ suffices (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).

\paragraph{Calibration does not resolve selection failures.}
Standard calibration methods (Platt scaling, temperature scaling) are monotonic transforms of LP that preserve the within-instance argmax and therefore cannot change selection outcomes.
Even a multi-feature variant (LP combined with token count and entity count), which breaks monotonicity, yields no significant selection improvement on any dataset ($p{=}0.31$--$0.83$; Table~\ref{tab:calibration}).
Calibration does reduce ECE substantially (from 0.26--0.39 to 0.01--0.08 under Platt scaling), but this improved probability estimation does not translate to better selection, consistent with the supervised combination result (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}) and the diagnosis that the bottleneck is LP-quality alignment rather than miscalibration (Appendix~\ref{app:calibration_baseline}).

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38), supporting selective prediction.
Quality estimation does not translate to selection, however: despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, no signal consistently outperforms greedy decoding.
The gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR selection fails because instance degeneracy (14\textendash 47\% identical outputs) eliminates headroom; and LP requires two jointly necessary conditions: low instance degeneracy, and adequate LP-quality alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).
When both conditions are met, LP achieves significant gains ($+1.36$~pp at 14\% degeneracy, $p{<}0.001$); when either is violated, selection fails.
Degeneracy is the dominant bottleneck, controllable via temperature and training budget; in the low-degeneracy regime, LP scales with sample count ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
Closing the gap for structural signals likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
\end{abstract}

73	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
74	\label{sec:selection_gap}
75	
76	We define the correlation-selection gap as the disparity between a signal's instance-level rank correlation with F1 and its ability to select the best output from $N$ candidates.
77	
78	Our argument proceeds in three layers.
79	First, four of five signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; they \textit{cannot} rank candidates within an instance by construction, and consensus-proximity (MBR) conversion does not reliably recover per-sample ranking.
80	Second, MBR selection with well-aligned utility (within-instance SJ--F1 $\rho{=}0.52$) should in principle select better outputs, but instance degeneracy collapses the candidate pool and eliminates the headroom MBR would otherwise exploit.
81	Third, LP, the sole natively per-sample signal, requires two jointly necessary conditions for effective selection: low degeneracy to provide exploitable headroom, and adequate LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}) \gtrsim 0.3$) to exploit it; compression (median range 0.041 nats) contributes but is not the sole bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
4	But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
5	
6	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
7	Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
8	Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we investigate \textit{why} this correlation fails to yield selection improvements, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
9	Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.
10	
11	A methodological premise structures our analysis: four of five signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) are instance-level aggregates that by design assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
12	These signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction and error flagging.
13	Yet quality estimation does not translate to structural selection, a disparity we term the \textbf{correlation-selection gap} (the disparity between a signal's ability to rank instances reliably and its failure to select the best output within a single instance): structural best-of-$N$ selection matches or degrades greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 12\textendash 14~pp oracle headroom.
14	The gap has two empirical causes: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, where fine-tuned models produce identical outputs for 14\textendash 47\% of instances, which eliminates selection headroom despite positive within-instance utility\textendash F1 correlation (median $\rho{=}0.52$); and (b)~\textit{weak LP-quality alignment}, where within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ is too low to exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
15	LP selection requires both low degeneracy and adequate alignment: significant at 13.8\% degeneracy with $\rho{\approx}0.5$ ($+1.36$~pp, $p{<}0.001$), sub-significant at 17.8\% with $\rho{\approx}0.24$ ($+0.42$~pp), and absent at 47.4\%.
16	
17	\begin{figure*}[t]
18	\centering
19	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
20	\caption{The correlation-selection gap. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably predict instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.45 on CoNLL, 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82). \textbf{Right}: quality estimation does not translate to selection; all methods approximately match greedy decoding ($T{=}0$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).}
21	\label{fig:overview}
22	\end{figure*}
23	
24	We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
25	We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
26	An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
27	Our contributions:
28	\begin{enumerate}
29	    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework.}
30	    We systematically evaluate five confidence signals from three families (structural, surface, model-internal) for LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, two model families, and a 4B scale ablation.
31	    Structural signals reliably predict output quality (VC $\rho{=}0.38$ on the primary test bed; EM AUROC${=}0.82$ on CoNLL), with difficulty-dependent but model-stable rankings that support selective prediction and error flagging.
32	
33	    \item \textbf{Diagnosis of the correlation-selection gap.}
34	    We identify a three-layer failure:
35	    (a)~four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates within an instance \textit{by construction};
36	    (b)~MBR selection with well-aligned utility (within-instance $\rho{=}0.52$) fails because instance degeneracy (14\textendash 47\% of instances yield identical outputs) collapses the candidate pool;
37	    (c)~LP, the sole per-sample signal, requires two jointly necessary conditions: low degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment ($\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}) \gtrsim 0.3$).
38	    A diagnostic chain (LoRA-rank ablation, free-form decoding, entity-token LP, supervised signal combination) confirms the bottleneck lies in the signal space accessible to unsupervised aggregation, not signal combination methods.
39	
40	    \item \textbf{Two necessary conditions for LP selection.}

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation and sample selection in LLM-based NER across four benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38 on the primary test bed, 0.42 on Few-NERD; AUROC up to 0.82), supporting selective prediction and error flagging.
However, quality estimation does not translate to sample selection, and the gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR selection with well-aligned utility ($\rho{=}0.52$) fails because instance degeneracy (14\textendash 47\%) collapses the candidate pool; and LP, the sole per-sample signal, requires two jointly necessary conditions: low degeneracy and adequate LP-quality alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).
LP selection succeeds when both conditions are met: at 13.8\% degeneracy with strong alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.5$; Few-NERD), LP achieves $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 17.8\% with weak alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.24$; SciERC), $+0.42$~pp ($p{=}0.091$); at 47.4\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
In the low-degeneracy regime, LP selection scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
Structural signals fail uniformly regardless of degeneracy, and supervised combination of all five signals cannot close the oracle gap; the bottleneck lies in the signal space accessible to unsupervised aggregation, not in the combination method.
Whether these patterns persist at 70B+ scales remains open.
Closing the gap for structural signals requires content-aware verifiers that examine output semantics \cite{cobbe2021verifiers}; LP provides a lightweight baseline when both degeneracy and alignment conditions are met.

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38), supporting selective prediction.
Quality estimation does not translate to selection, however: despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, no signal consistently outperforms greedy decoding.
The gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; MBR selection fails because instance degeneracy (14\textendash 47\% identical outputs) eliminates headroom; and LP requires two jointly necessary conditions: low instance degeneracy, and adequate LP-quality alignment ($\rho \gtrsim 0.3$).
When both conditions are met, LP achieves significant gains ($+1.36$~pp at 14\% degeneracy, $p{<}0.001$); when either is violated, selection fails.
Degeneracy is the dominant bottleneck, controllable via temperature and training budget; in the low-degeneracy regime, LP scales with sample count ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
Closing the gap for structural signals likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
\end{abstract}

\section{Few-NERD Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}

\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+2.95$~pp (0.748 $\to$ 0.777) but nearly triples instance degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 31.3\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs from 85.6\% to 68.7\%.
LP selection gains drop correspondingly ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp), consistent with the degeneracy-gating mechanism identified in the main text (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Within-instance LP-quality alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (mean $\rho$: $0.524 \to 0.407$; median $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with alignment being determined primarily by task structure rather than training duration.

Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3 (0.032 $\to$ 0.041 at epoch 5), and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at step 32{,}000 (approximately epoch 3.9).
Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime where LP selection is most effective.
This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.
